item.title: Design of Functional Modules in PBAT Molecular Structure and Their Performance Investigation
item.description:
Abstract
Fully biodegradable materials are of paramount importance in addressing the global “white pollution” crisis owing to their excellent degradation properties. Poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) (PBAT), which exhibits good thermal stability, excellent impact toughness, and outstanding biodegradability, is widely recognized as one of the most promising alternatives to nonbiodegradable commodity plastics such as conventional polyethylene. Nevertheless, the mechanical properties, molecular weight, photostability, and processing properties of PBAT still require further optimization. Herein, during the synthesis of PBAT, branched structural units and photostabilizing units were incorporated into its molecular chains to enhance its mechanical properties and photostability. The results showed that when 1,2-hexanediol was used as the branching unit, the tensile strength of the synthesized branched PBAT increased from 27.3 to 49.1 MPa, the intrinsic viscosity increased to 1.77 dL·g–1, and the melt flow index decreased to 3.1 g·(10 min)−1; when the photostabilizer content was 0.3%, the weight-average molecular weight reached 14.4 × 104 g·mol–1. After ultraviolet aging, the tensile strength retention was as high as 24.5%, and the elongation at break retention was 10.5%, demonstrating excellent photostability. The successful incorporation of functional modules into PBAT molecular chains provides an effective approach for improving both mechanical properties and photostability. The enhanced resistance to UV aging enables better property retention during service, which may help extend the usable lifetime of PBAT-based products and support the broader application of biodegradable polymers in practical environments.

item.title: The Competitive Evolution of Oxygen-Containing Functional Groups during Pressure-Controlled Pyrolysis of Oil Shale
item.description:
Abstract
Oil shale serves as a vital strategic alternative fossil energy resource for China. Uncovering how graded pressures govern the cleavage and conversion of diverse oxygen-bearing structures helps to understand pressure-modulated kerogen transformation at the chemical-bond level and enriches the microscopic theoretical framework of pressure-regulated oil-generation processes. This work focuses on competitive evolution of oxygen-containing functional groups in solid-phase pyrolysis residues. In this work, continental Type II1–I oil shale sampled from Huadian, Jilin Province was subjected to pressure-controlled pyrolysis at 400 °C for 240 min under pressures ranging from atmospheric pressure to 8.0 MPa. A combined characterization platform integrating Gaussian peak-fitting Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy(FTIR), Thermogravimetry (TG) and Gas Chromatography–Mass Spectrometry (GC-MS) was adopted to characterize evolutionary behaviors of three typical oxygen-containing functional group bands. Combined with TG-DTG and GC-MS auxiliary evidence, carbonyl-related structures show a tendency of enhanced retention near 2 MPa. High-pressure treatment preserves aliphatic oil-generating precursors and elevates thermal stability of pyrolysis residues, accompanied by an increasing relative abundance of medium-long-chain alkanes within collected liquid shale-oil fractions. This study establishes correlations among solid-phase microstructures, macroscopic thermal weight-loss behaviors and relative compositional features of liquid pyrolytic products, providing fundamental microscale experimental observations and mechanistic references for laboratory-scale pressurized oil-shale pyrolysis research.

item.title: Covalent Attachment of Superoxide Dismutase to Phospholipid Membranes: A Nanoarchitectonics Strategy for Preparing Liposome–Enzyme Complexes
item.description:
Abstract
Superoxide dismutase (SOD) is a biologically important antioxidant enzyme and various strategies have been employed to immobilize SOD at material interfaces. However, there has been limited exploration of SOD attachment to lipid membranes despite emerging interest in SOD-liposome systems. Addressing this gap would improve physicochemical understanding of how attachment chemistry affects SOD-membrane interactions and could guide practical applications. Herein, we explored two strategies for attaching SOD to supported lipid bilayer (SLB) platforms in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) conditions by comparing covalent and noncovalent approaches based on maleimide–thiol chemistry and electrostatic-mediated adsorption, respectively. Quartz crystal microbalance-dissipation (QCM-D) experiments revealed stable SOD attachment to SLBs via the covalent strategy, whereas there was minimal noncovalent adsorption on positively charged SLBs despite the net negative charge of SOD. These results led us to further investigate the covalent strategy by preparing SOD-liposome complexes. Dynamic light scattering (DLS) and electrophoretic mobility measurements identified a suitable range of enzyme-to-lipid ratios where colloidal stability was maintained. At higher ratios, the onset of apparent liposome aggregation coincided with decreased zeta potential magnitude. Importantly, liposome-conjugated SOD retained enzymatic activity, demonstrating that maleimide–thiol chemistry is an effective strategy to covalently conjugate SOD to lipid membrane interfaces and prepare colloidally stable liposome-enzyme complexes that exhibit antioxidant activity. Based on these findings, we discuss how charge screening likely aids the covalent strategy while attenuating noncovalent adsorption, highlighting the interplay between chemical conjugation and interfacial forces to modulate SOD attachment to lipid membranes.

item.title: Utilization of Sludge-Derived Slag in Magnesium Oxychloride Cement Composites: A Pathway to Green Construction Materials
item.description:
Abstract
Magnesium oxychloride cement (MOC) represents a promising alternative to Portland cement due to its lower carbon footprint, rapid strength development, and favorable mechanical properties. This study investigates sludge-derived slag (SDS), a byproduct of plasma gasification of wastewater sludge, as a partial, full, or excessive replacement of silica sand filler in MOC composites. SDS was characterized in terms of its chemical and phase composition, microstructure, and particle size distribution, and subsequently incorporated into MOC mixtures (50–200 wt % replacement). The incorporation of SDS led to a progressive densification of the composite structure, reflected by increased bulk and specific density (up to ∼6.6% and ∼3.5%, respectively) and reduced total porosity (up to ∼18.5%). These changes resulted in improved mechanical performance, with compressive strength increasing by ∼11.9%, flexural strength by up to ∼33.6%, and Young’s modulus by ∼25.2%. Additionally, reduced water absorption and capillary transport indicated improved resistance to moisture ingress. Overall, the results confirm that SDS can effectively replace natural aggregate without compromising performance, while often enhancing key properties. As a secondary material from plasma waste processing, SDS contributes to waste valorization and reduces reliance on natural aggregates, whose availability is increasingly limited. The developed MOC-SDS composites thus represent a promising eco-efficient material for sustainable construction.

item.title: Integrated Geological-Dynamic Analysis and Development Optimization of Interlayer Connectivity in an Offshore Calcareous-Barrier-Controlled Stacked Reservoir
item.description:
Abstract
Heterogeneous barriers influence pressure support and water entry in offshore stacked reservoirs, but their development implications are difficult to evaluate where well control in the upper zone is sparse. This study integrates drilled barrier interpretation, operation-screened production dynamics, geological monitoring priorities, and reservoir simulation for Zone B and the underlying Zone C of the LFA field. The mixed clastic–carbonate barrier becomes thinner and more calcareous-sandstone-rich northward and thicker and more limestone-dominated southward. Drilled barrier intervals are 0.63–2.50 m thick, with interpreted permeabilities of 0.05–1.50 mD where available. Production records through 28 February 2026 show a positive association between A10H and the screened Zone C common factor (r = 0.554, n = 549), while the residual association of every candidate well becomes indistinguishable from zero once the shared Zone C signal is removed. A conductance-and-spacing prior, evaluated across 1,107 scenarios, consistently places A8H, A1H, A6H, and A2H in the upper monitoring group, followed by A5H. These observations support thin-barrier, transition, and thick-barrier development domains within combined edge–bottom-water and edge-water-drive interpretations. Field-history-matched 1-, 5-, and 9-well schemes forecast Zone B recovery factors of 10.2%, 30.8%, and approximately 37% by 2045, with approximately 1.51 × 106 m3 of cumulative Zone B oil production in the full scheme. Subsequent early production from A18H, A19H, and A20M spports the implemented thick-barrier and transition-domain deployment. The workflow connects barrier heterogeneity and the scale of dynamic evidence to traceable monitoring and phased development decisions without equating production association with direct hydraulic validation.

item.title: Charge Ratio and Distribution Effects on Lys/Ala Peptide Conformation and Adsorption onto the Lipid Bilayer Membrane (POPS)
item.description:
Abstract
In the present work, molecular dynamics simulations were performed to investigate peptide samples composed of lysine (Lys) and alanine (Ala) residues interacting with an anionic lipid bilayer membrane. We systematically examined how the sequence pattern, lysine content, and charge distribution along the peptide chain govern the structural properties and their adsorption onto the 1-palmitoyl-2-oleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phospho-L-serine (POPS) membrane. Our results reveal that both the radius of gyration (Rg) and the root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) increase with chain length, reflecting greater conformational entropy in longer chains. The scaling exponent ν derived from the power-law analysis of Rg indicates that the peptide chains adopt highly extended conformations. Notably, ν decreases with increasing lysine ratio of the peptide chain, which can be rationalized by the competition between intrachain electrostatic repulsion and membrane-induced electrostatic anchoring. Root-mean-square fluctuation (RMSF) analysis reveals a characteristic double-well profile, with overall flexibility increasing with chain length, and lysine residues consistently exhibit higher local flexibility than alanine. Simulation results also show that peptides with the same charge ratio but different spatial distributions exhibit distinct conformational dynamics and membrane adsorption behavior, demonstrating that the spatial distribution of charged Lys residues, rather than chain length or net charge, governs peptide–membrane contacts and adsorption kinetics. Increasing the Lys fraction strengthens electrostatic anchoring, promotes peptide extension along the membrane plane, and restricts motion normal to the membrane, resulting in pronounced conformational anisotropy. In terms of adsorption, the all-Ala peptide cannot adsorb stably, whereas Lys-containing peptides adsorb stably onto the POPS membrane, with faster adsorption at higher Lys content up to 75%. These findings may provide clear design principles for tuning peptide conformation and membrane adsorption by controlling charge ratio and spatial distribution, and ultimately offer a practical possibility for their application in biotechnology.

item.title: A Heated-Radius Calculation Model for Multicomponent Thermal Fluid Huff-and-Puff in Heavy Oil Reservoirs
item.description:
Abstract
Multicomponent thermal fluid consists of several gaseous components, and the actual temperature distribution within the heated zone is nonisothermal, rendering the Marx–Langenheim isothermal heating model inapplicable. In this study, based on the energy release behavior of multicomponent thermal fluid during the heating of the oil reservoir, the heated zone is partitioned into a latent-heat zone and a sensible-heat zone, and a heated-radius calculation model is developed in accordance with the energy conservation principle. The results indicate that the predictions from the proposed model match well with the CMG simulation results, with relative errors ranging from 0.23% to 3.32%. In the process of multicomponent thermal fluid huff-and-puff development, increasing steam quality and injection amount while decreasing noncondensable gas (NCG) content can effectively expand the heated radius. Moreover, the heated radius increases with an increasing number of huff-and-puff cycles, with residual formation heat being the primary driver of this continuous enlargement. Among the reservoir parameters examined, the equivalent volumetric heat capacity and thickness of the reservoir were found to have the most pronounced influence on the heated radius. This study provides a theoretical foundation for predicting the heating radius and optimizing parameters in multicomponent thermal fluid huff-and-puff operations.

item.title: Casting-Derived PVA/PDMS Janus Membranes with Stable Photothermal Conversion for Solar Desalination
item.description:
Abstract
Solar photothermal conversion enables water evaporation and purification through localized interfacial heating, offering a sustainable approach for solar energy utilization. However, integrating efficient solar harvesting, continuous water transport, and structural support within a simply fabricated membrane remains challenging. In this study, a casting-derived Janus bilayer photothermal membrane was developed by integrating a hydrophilic PVA/FeCo@C/CNTs/ACNTs photothermal layer with a hydrophobic PDMS/ZnO nanorod supporting layer. The multicomponent FeCo@C/CNTs/ACNTs photothermal layer provides strong broadband solar absorption and efficient photothermal conversion, while the PVA matrix facilitates continuous water transport through swelling-assisted hydration. Meanwhile, the PDMS/ZnO nanorod layer provides mechanical support for the PVA-based photothermal layer and contributes to the structural integrity of the bilayer membrane during interfacial evaporation. Under 1.5 sun irradiation, the membrane surface temperature reached 83.7 °C, while an evaporation rate of 1.618 kg·m–2·h–1 was achieved under 1 sun irradiation. In addition, the membrane demonstrated effective performance in solar-driven seawater desalination and dye-containing water purification, highlighting its potential for solar-driven water-treatment applications.

item.title: Effect of Iminodiacetic Acid on the Temporal Dependence of Chromium Sorption in Poly(ethylene glycol)-Based Hydrogels
item.description:
Abstract
Chromium remains a persistent concern because of its industrial use and its risks to ecosystems and human health. Its behavior and toxicity depend on its chemical speciation, mainly on its oxidation states Cr(III) and Cr(VI). Speciation analysis remains a challenge, and the proposal of innovative materials as substitutes for solid-phase extractors or preconcentrators is relevant. However, the sorption pathways and ligand-induced changes in hydrogel matrices remain less understood. In this work, poly(ethylene glycol)-based hydrogels were prepared by modification with glycidyl methacrylate and cross-linked with N,N′-methylenebis(acrylamide). The hydrogel properties were characterized by swelling, scanning electron microscopy, Brunauer–Emmett–Teller surface area, and point of zero charge determination. We found that after incorporation of iminodiacetic acid, the internal structure of the hydrogel changed, increasing pore size from mostly below 5 μm to approximately 100 μm and decreasing the surface area from 566 to 229 m2 g–1. In addition, the point of zero charge remained close to pH 7.0 for both materials. Chromium sorption assays revealed higher affinity for Cr(III) than for Cr(VI). Compared to the control hydrogel, the presence of iminodiacetic acid in the hydrogels delayed Cr(VI) sorption; uptake began only after approximately 300 min, achieving about 40% after 1440 min. Cr(III) sorption followed pseudo-second-order behavior combined with intraparticle diffusion after iminodiacetic acid incorporation, whereas Cr(VI) sorption was better described by the Avrami model, indicating a complex multistep process. Adsorption isotherm data showed that the Freundlich model best described chromium sorption by both hydrogels. Acid desorption assays demonstrated a virtually quantitative release of Cr(III) from the control hydrogel but only about 72% from the hydrogel containing iminodiacetic acid, corroborating stronger retention of Cr(III) via chelation. These results show that iminodiacetic acid incorporation modulates not only chromium affinity but also the sorption kinetics in poly(ethylene glycol)-based hydrogels.

item.title: Defect Engineering and Phase Modulation in Fe-Doped TiO 2 Nanocrystals: Unraveling the Origin of Enhanced Visible-Light Absorption
item.description:
Abstract
Engineering lattice distortion and electronic structure is a promising strategy for tailoring the functional properties of semiconductor nanocrystals. Herein, Fe-doped TiO2 nanocrystals containing 0–1.0 wt % Fe were synthesized via a wet-chemical route to investigate the interplay between Fe incorporation, phase evolution, and optical properties. X-ray diffraction and Rietveld refinement revealed anatase/brookite heterophase nanocrystals without detectable secondary iron oxide phases, indicating no discernible phase segregation. Fe incorporation promoted brookite stabilization at low dopant concentrations and systematically modified crystallite size, crystallinity, and lattice microstrain. Raman and FTIR analyses revealed increasing local disorder and distortion of the TiO6 coordination environment. These structural changes were accompanied by enhanced visible-light absorption and a reduction in the optical band gap from 3.00 to 2.60 eV. Crystal-field analysis yielded a splitting energy of ∼1.92 eV, supporting Fe3+ ions in distorted octahedral oxygen environments. Notably, the correlation between lattice microstrain and band gap energy demonstrates the role of dopant-induced structural distortion in modulating the electronic structure of TiO2. These findings establish controlled Fe incorporation as an effective approach for tuning the structural and optical properties of TiO2 nanocrystals for visible-light-driven photocatalysis, optoelectronics, and solar energy applications.

item.title: Microfabrication via Two-Photon Cross-Linking: An Investigation of Fabrication Parameters
item.description:
Abstract
Two-photon lithography (2PL) is a microfabrication technique that has become a standard method for the generation of miniaturized 3D objects. A promising novel approach to laser direct writing is two-photon cross-linking (2PC), which uses thin solid films of copolymers containing small amounts of chromophores acting as a two-photon cross-linker. Upon activation by two-photon light absorption, they form polymer networks through cross-linking via C–H insertion (CHic) at the focal point of the laser beam. As the focal volume moves, polymer structures are written into the film as a latent image. In all regions outside the focal point where cross-linking has not occurred, the polymer is completely removed by extraction with a suitable solvent. The quality of the fabricated structures is determined by the size and overlap of the voxels that constitute the structure and their arrangement, which can be adjusted through parameters such as beam intensity, scan speed, and a proper choice of slicing and hatching. On the one hand, the yield of the photochemical cross-linking process in the voxel needs to be high enough so that percolation is reached; on the other hand, the input of excessive energy must be avoided to prevent photodegradation of the forming structures. In this work, we present a model of the 2PC process, which describes the conditions under which high-resolution 3D structures can be obtained.

item.title: Mechanistic Insights into CO 2 Photoreduction to HCOOH on BH- and NH-Modified g-C 3 N 4 -Based Photocatalysts
item.description:
Abstract
Graphitic carbon nitride (g-C3N4) is an attractive metal-free platform for the photocatalytic conversion of CO2 into value-added products, but its activity is limited by poor visible-light absorption, fast electron–hole recombination, and the intrinsic inertness of the CO2 molecule. This computational study employs density functional theory (DFT) and its time-dependent formulation (TD-DFT), complemented by multistate CASPT2 calculations, to map a complete CO2 photoreduction pathway toward formic acid (HCOOH) on a triheptazine (THZ) model bearing BH and NH substitutions. CO2 activation is found to occur spontaneously in the electronic ground state (S0), but only under cooperative adsorption, in which the boron-containing fragment binds H2O while the NH-substituted fragment accepts an electron from the photocatalyst, producing a bent CO2– radical anion; no activation is observed on the unsubstituted THZ. Along the reaction pathway, three energy barriers are too high to be surmounted thermally, namely C–C bond cleavage (2.05 eV), C–O bond cleavage (0.69 eV), and water reformation at the boron site (1.18 eV). These barriers are surmounted by light excitation to the S1 state. For each of them, a conical intersection between the S0 and S1 potential energy surfaces was located in the vicinity of the preceding intermediate. These crossings provide efficient nonradiative funnels driving the system over each barrier. The results show that controlled BH and NH substitution couples visible-light absorption, charge separation, and excited-state energy funneling within a single metal-free model, while preserving the substitution pattern responsible for absorption throughout the catalytic cycle.

item.title: Q-Planner: A Harness System for Quantum Chemistry Agents
item.description:
Abstract
LLM-based agents for computational chemistry commonly place the model inside an accumulating execution loop, causing context growth proportional to workflow length, unpredictable token costs, and degraded plan reliability at scale. We present a chemistry computation harness that confines LLM invocations to three semantically bounded stages─compound identification, planning, and reporting─while delegating all tool dispatch, parallel scheduling, arithmetic derivation, and artifact routing to a deterministic LangGraph executor that consumes zero LLM tokens during execution; a library of domain skill modules injects specialist quantum chemistry protocols into the planner context at planning time without enlarging the execution context. Across five representative quantum chemistry workflows, the planning, calculator, and reporting calls averaged 9700–25,300 tokens per run, with zero execution-stage tokens in every case─more than 93% fewer tokens (before caching) than loop-based multiagent systems─and, on a high-throughput single-point-energy scaling benchmark, a full-scheme plan representation sustained 100% plan-structural correctness across all 30 runs from N = 10 to 100 compounds of one workflow type, generating a 200-node graph of 100 independent single-point jobs from a single planning call. On the workloads tested, harness design made quantum chemistry automation more robust and its cost more predictable; the model ablation shows that model capability still matters.

item.title: Tree-Based Classification of Functional Groups from IR Spectra: Feature Importance Corroborates Quantum-Chemical Fragment Frequencies
item.description:
Abstract
Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy is a widely used analytical technique for identifying functional groups (FGs) in chemical compounds, but its interpretation remains labor-intensive and reliant on expert knowledge, especially for complex or multicomponent samples. This study presents a tree-based random forest (RF) machine-learning framework, successfully developed to predict the presence of specific FG from an infrared spectra database. Stratification was employed to address positive class imbalance, maintaining the F1-score drop under 12% across models. All models achieved strong overall performance, with accuracy, F1-score, ROC-AUC, and out-of-bag (OOB) scores exceeding 0.8. Of the 46 FGs modeled, 43 demonstrated acceptable performance, while only three underperformed, as categorized by their Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) and precision-recall area under the curve (PR-AUC) scores. Threshold tuning further improved model performance, yielding up to a 9% increase in MCC score. Finally, feature importance extracted from the trained models exhibited strong interpretability, correlating with theoretically predicted IR spectra and bridging experimental data with theoretical chemical significance. These results establish a robust, interpretable framework with potential for integration into intelligent monitoring and process optimization systems.

item.title: Riboflavin–Ceria Nanoparticles Induce ROS-Driven Mitochondrial Dysfunction in Breast Cancer
item.description:
Abstract
Cerium oxide nanoparticles (CeO2 NPs) are redox-active nanomaterials with emerging potential in cancer therapy, although their limited cytotoxicity and insufficient mechanistic understanding hinder clinical application. Here, we developed riboflavin-functionalized CeO2 nanoparticles (Rf-CeO2) to enhance photodynamic anticancer efficacy via controlled reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation and mitochondrial targeting. Rf conjugation improves nanoparticle stability and enables photodynamic activation under UV irradiation leading to elevated intracellular oxidative stress. In MDA-MB-231 breast cancer cells, Rf-CeO2 exhibits significantly enhanced cytotoxicity compared to pristine CeO2, inducing dose-dependent cell death and apoptosis. This effect is markedly potentiated by UV exposure, consistent with increased ROS-mediated oxidative stress. Proteomic analysis identifies 60 differentially expressed proteins, revealing disruptions of metabolic pathways, protein synthesis, and DNA repair. Notably, citrate synthase (CS), a key enzyme in the tricarboxylic acid cycle, is significantly downregulated and associated with poor prognosis in breast cancer. Functional validation using Seahorse Mito Stress and TMRM assays confirms mitochondrial dysfunction, including impaired oxidative phosphorylation, reduced ATP production, and loss of membrane potential. Overall, these results demonstrate that Rf-CeO2 acts as an effective photodynamic nanoplatform that induces cancer cell death through synergistic ROS generation and mitochondrial metabolic disruption. This study provides new proteomic insights into ceria-based nanotherapeutics and highlights citrate synthase as a potential therapeutic target for breast cancer.

item.title: Integrated In Silico and In Vivo Toxicogenetic Assessment of Piperine and 4,5-Dihydroxypiperine in Drosophila melanogaster
item.description:
Abstract
4,5-Dihydroxypiperine (dhPIP) is a synthetic derivative of piperine (PIP), a bioactive alkaloid investigated as a phytogenic additive. This study evaluated the in vitro antioxidant capacity, in silico pharmacokinetic, and in vivo toxicogenetics of PIP and dhPIP using standard (ST) and high-bioactivation (HB) crosses of Drosophila melanogaster. DhPIP exhibited higher antioxidant activity than PIP. In silico, high intestinal absorption and low blood–brain barrier permeability was predicted for both, but CYP450 interactions were exclusive to PIP. In vivo, neither compound was genotoxic. Notably, both alkaloids reduced doxorubicin-induced DNA damage. In the ST cross, PIP inhibited 92–98% of genotoxicity, dropping to 51–55% in the HB cross. Conversely, dhPIP reduced damage by approximately 50% in both crosses. These findings demonstrate that PIP and dhPIP lack genotoxic effects, highlighting that while dhPIP offers enhanced antioxidant capacity, its in vivo antigenotoxicity is lower than PIP’s but remains unaffected by CYP450-mediated metabolism.

item.title: Defect-Engineered Al- and Nd-Doped WO 3 Films for Enhanced Carbon Monoxide Sensing via Oxygen Vacancy Modulation
item.description:
Abstract
Carbon monoxide (CO) is a highly toxic, colorless, and odorless gas that poses a serious risk to human health, making its reliable detection essential for environmental monitoring and industrial safety. In this work, defect-engineered WO3 films, pure, single-doped, and codoped with Al3+ and Nd3+ were developed to enhance CO sensing at an operating temperature of 200 °C. Synergistic defect engineering was achieved through simultaneous Al and Nd codoping, which enables controlled modulation of oxygen vacancies, charge transport, and surface reactivity. The materials were synthesized via a coprecipitation-assisted ultrasonic method and deposited as films using the Doctor Blade technique. structural, optical, morphological, and electrical characterizations (X-ray diffraction (XRD), Raman, UV–Vis, PL, Scanning electron microscopy (SEM), AFM, and electrical measurements) revealed that Al3+ doping promotes lattice distortion and increased defect density, particularly oxygen vacancies, while Nd3+ induces improved crystallinity and structural relaxation. Gas sensing measurements indicated that all WO3-based sensors responded to CO. Pure WO3 exhibited the highest response (47.37%), followed by WO3–Al (26.31%), WO3–Nd (15.10%), and WO3–AlNd (14.56%) at 200 °C. Notably, all doped WO3 sensors exhibited higher CO responses than the commercial MQ-135 sensor (5.95%) under the same experimental conditions. Among the doped materials, WO3–Al exhibited the superior response, whereas WO3–AlNd showed a balanced combination of response and recovery characteristics, which may be associated with the combined effects of defect modulation and charge transport. Compared with pure WO3, the doped WO3 sensors exhibited faster sensing dynamics, with response and recovery times: 73–31, 27–44, 35–44, and 28–40, respectively. These results highlight the potential of doped WO3 sensors as promising materials for CO sensing applications.

item.title: Agglomerate Size Tuning of Cathode Catalyst Layers Fabricated Using Electrospray Deposition and Its Effects on PEMFC Performance
item.description:
Abstract
The catalyst layers in proton-exchange membrane fuel cells comprise agglomerates of Pt/C and ionomers, and their size may affect the catalyst layer structure and electrochemical properties. However, it is difficult to vary the agglomerate size without changing the composition of the catalyst layer. This study investigated a method for modifying the agglomerate size during catalyst layer fabrication using electrospray deposition and evaluated its effect on cell performance through single-cell testing. The agglomerate size was measured by varying the needle diameter, ink flow rate, Pt/C concentration in the solvent, and solvent type. The results showed that the differences associated with solvent selection produced the largest changes in agglomerate size among the investigated parameters. At a common flow rate of 0.4 mL h–1, the mean agglomerate diameters obtained using methanol and 2-propanol were 146 and 376 nm, respectively. Scanning electron microscopy observations revealed the presence of relatively large pores in the catalyst layer prepared using 2-propanol. This layer exhibited superior oxygen transport characteristics and a higher power output than the methanol-based layer, particularly when air was supplied to the cathode. In contrast, the methanol-based layer produced a higher power output when pure oxygen was used. These results demonstrate that electrospray deposition can produce catalyst layers with different agglomerate sizes and pore structures without altering the catalyst layer composition, thereby changing their electrochemical and transport properties.

item.title: Methyl Jasmonate and γ-Aminobutyric Acid as Attenuators of Salt Stress in Sunflower
item.description:
Abstract
Foliar application of stress-mitigating biomolecules, such as methyl jasmonate (MJ) and γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA), is a promising strategy to protect plant physiology under salinity stress. However, it remains unclear whether their combined application provides benefits beyond those of each compound alone in oilseed crops. This study evaluated MJ and GABA, applied alone and in combination, as attenuators of salt stress in sunflower (Helianthus annuus L., cv. BRS 323). A greenhouse experiment was conducted in a randomized block design with a 3 × 4 factorial arrangement: three electrical conductivities of the irrigation water (ECw: 0.5, 3.5, and 6.5 dS m–1) and four foliar treatments (control, MJ at 1 mM, GABA at 2 mM, and MJ + GABA). We also decomposed the attenuator factor into a 2 × 2 factorial (MJ × GABA) to test for synergistic effects. Salinity at 6.5 dS m–1 reduced plant height by 29%, total dry mass by 41%, and net CO2 assimilation (A) by 37%; in untreated plants, it also reduced the maximum quantum efficiency of photosystem II (Fv/Fm) by 26% and nearly doubled leaf Na+ content. Regardless of salinity, GABA increased stem dry mass by 16%, total dry mass by 15%, and A by 20%. In contrast, MJ + GABA increased capitulum dry mass by 21%, A by 22%, and water-use efficiency by 20% relative to untreated plants. At 6.5 dS m–1, GABA and MJ + GABA increased Fv/Fm by 7–9% and relative water content by 38–40%, and all attenuators reduced leaf Na+ content by 29–47%, with MJ alone being the most effective. The MJ × GABA interaction was not significant for most traits. Responses to the combined treatment were largely driven by GABA, with no consistent evidence of synergistic benefits. Therefore, GABA, alone or combined with MJ, is the most promising option among those tested for mitigating salt stress in sunflower, although field validation, including seed and oil yield, is still required.

item.title: Designing an Open-Source Multi-Vat Digital Light Processing Printer
item.description:
Abstract
Additive manufacturing has undergone rapid evolution in modalities that can mimic some of the aspect of native human tissue architectures with high resolution. Among these emerging approaches, digital light processing (DLP)-based printing enables the fabrication of intricate biomimetic architectures through the photopolymerization of polymer-based hydrogels. The recent emergence of multivat printing further enhances this capability, enabling the spatial arrangement of differently formulated or labeled photocrosslinkable resins. However, the widespread adoption of DLP printing remains constrained by the high cost, proprietary hardware, and limited customizability of commercially available systems. Here, we present an open-source multivat DLP printing platform developed through the integration and modification of two low-cost commercially available 3D printers. A dedicated Python-based graphical user interface was developed, providing user-defined control over critical printing parameters, including exposure time, layer height, printing sequence, and vat switching. Comprehensive hardware documentation and a complete bill of materials (BOM) are provided to ensure reproducibility and accessibility across research laboratories. In addition to multivat printing, the system enables spatial modulation of mechanical properties within a single photocrosslinkable formulation through programmable light exposure and supports enhanced z-axis resolution through user-defined layer thickness control. The platform was validated through the fabrication of geometrically complex, multivat, and mechanically heterogeneous constructs. Collectively, this work establishes an accessible and customizable DLP printing platform that enables advanced hydrogel fabrication and demonstrates automated multivat printing.

item.title: Design, Synthesis, In Silico, and Biological Evaluation of Novel Chalcone–Benzamide Conjugates as Alkaline Phosphatase Inhibitors
item.description:
Abstract
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP) is a zinc-dependent metalloenzyme that catalyzes the hydrolysis of phosphate monoesters and is essential to several important physiological processes, such as bone mineralization and signal transduction. The clinical correlation of dysregulated ALP activity with a wide range of disease types, including bone disorders, hepatobiliary diseases, and certain malignancies, highlights the therapeutic importance of developing and identifying potent calf intestinal alkaline phosphatase (CIALP) inhibitors. Eleven new chalcone–benzamide derivatives (3a–3k), containing structurally different substituents, were synthesized and extensively investigated by spectroscopic methods such as IR, 1H NMR, 13C NMR, and low-resolution EI-MS analysis. All synthesized compounds were screened for DPPH radical-scavenging activity, with ascorbic acid as the standard (IC50 = 18.68 μM), and CIALP inhibitory activity, with KH2PO4 as the standard (IC50 = 2.80 ± 0.065 μM). In the DPPH assay, compound 3k showed the highest antioxidant activity (IC50 = 21.21 μM), followed by 3h (29.94 μM), 3j (39.92 μM), and 3c (53.22 μM), closest to the reference standard. In the enzyme inhibition assay, compounds 3d (IC50 = 3.93 ± 0.314 μM), 3h (IC50 = 4.49 ± 1.312 μM), and 3c (IC50 = 5.69 ± 1.124 μM) demonstrated the most potent enzyme inhibitory activities. Docking of the synthesized compounds was performed against the crystal structure of placental alkaline phosphatase (PLAP, PDB ID: 1EW2), used as a structural homologue in the absence of a deposited CIALP crystal structure, which showed that all synthesized compounds had good binding energies ranging from −7.9 to −8.3 kcal/mol; this narrow range is within the resolution limits of AutoDock scoring and did not correlate with experimental enzyme-inhibitory potency across the series. Prioritized lead candidates were found to have good oral bioavailability (expected to be above 90% absorption), acceptable physicochemical properties (compliant with Lipinski’s rule of five), and manageable toxicity risk. Together, the integrated in vitro biological and in silico computational data suggested that compounds 3h, 3c, and 3j are promising dual-function leads with both antioxidant and enzyme-inhibitory activity, while compound 3d stands out as a potent, structurally distinct enzyme inhibitor─making the benzamide scaffold a promising structural framework for the rational optimization of multitarget therapeutics.

item.title: Application of Fully Automated Filtration for Precipitation Polymerizations in Synthesis Robots
item.description:
Abstract
A tailor-made, low-cost filtration module was implemented into a synthesis robot to perform automated sampling during precipitation polymerizations, enabling a direct analysis via gas chromatography (GC). Furthermore, a custom-developed computational workflow was created to automate the processing of raw chromatographic data, leading to an automated evaluation of the reaction progress. For this purpose, a standard septum-piercing needle was modified to fit onto a syringe filter. A rack was designed to hold the sampling vial with a syringe filter attached to it. A spring was utilized to enable a tight fixation of the needle, and a metal block was placed above the rack to ensure safe removal of the needle. To validate the new setup, six precipitation polymerizations were performed. Three of these were purified with the novel automated filtration procedure directly after sampling. The remaining underwent manual filtration of the collected samples at the end of the reaction, enabling a comparison between both approaches. The automated sampling process was highly reproducible and time- as well as work-efficient.

item.title: Biogenic Silver Nanoparticles from Penicillium chrysogenum Incorporated in Polymeric Micelles: Antimicrobial Activity and Cytotoxicity Evaluation
item.description:
Abstract
Biogenic silver nanoparticles (AgNPs) are investigated for their antimicrobial activity and reduced toxicity associated with metabolite-derived surface coatings. Their stability and biological activity are enhanced by metabolite-derived coatings produced by the synthesizing organism. This study develops hybrid nanocarriers by combining biogenic AgNPs synthesized from Penicillium chrysogenum with poloxamer micelles. Subsequently, the AgNPs were incorporated into poloxamer-based micelles (PL188 and PL407), yielding the nanocarriers AgNPs_PL407 and AgNPs_PL188. Physicochemical characterization was performed using dynamic light scattering (DLS) to determine hydrodynamic diameter (Dh), polydispersity index (PDI), and zeta potential (ζ). Antimicrobial activity was evaluated through disk-diffusion assays, minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC), and bacterial growth kinetics. Cell viability was assessed using trypan blue exclusion and MTS (3-(4,5-dimethylthiazol-2-yl)-5-(3-carboxymethoxyphenyl)-2-(4-sulfophenyl)-2H-tetrazolium) assays. Biogenic AgNPs exhibited a Dh of 277.20 ± 112.16 nm, a PDI of 0.271, and a ζ potential of −9.40 ± 0.54 mV. Pure poloxamers showed ζ potentials close to zero (0.03 ± 0.07 mV and −0.01 ± 0.06 mV, respectively). Incorporation resulted in AgNPs_PL407 nanocarriers, characterized by greater heterogeneity, with a Dh of 555.60 ± 268.40 nm and a PDI of 1.000, and in AgNPs_PL188 nanocarriers, characterized by greater homogeneity, with a Dh of 301.63 ± 106.11 nm and a PDI of 0.349. Both hybrid systems exhibited ζ potentials near zero (−0.02 ± 0.00 mV for AgNPs_PL407 and −0.00 ± 0.00 mV for AgNPs_PL188), indicating the possible colloidal stabilization conferred by the poloxamers. Both the AgNPs and the hybrid nanocarriers demonstrated antimicrobial activity across the tested combinations, supporting their broad antimicrobial potential. Importantly, most antimicrobial MIC values were below the cytotoxicity threshold determined for HaCaT cells (IC50 = 2.29 × 1010 NPs/mL), particularly those obtained for the hybrid nanocarriers. However, free AgNPs against E. coli showed an MIC of 2.65 × 1010 NPs/mL, slightly exceeding the HaCaT IC50, indicating that the apparent therapeutic window was formulation- and microorganism-dependent. Cytotoxicity assays also confirmed high cell viability at biologically active concentrations, particularly for the hybrid systems. AgNPs_PL188 showed the most promising overall profile, combining favorable antibacterial performance with low apparent cytotoxicity. Overall, these results suggest that incorporating biogenic AgNPs into poloxamer micelles may improve their apparent antimicrobial selectivity over cytotoxicity, highlighting their potential for developing antimicrobial formulations, particularly for oral inhalation administration. However, further studies are needed to optimize the system and ensure product safety.

item.title: From MRI Contrast to Compatibility: Distinct Macrophage and Neutrophil Responses to Metal Oxide Nanoparticles versus Gadobutrol
item.description:
Abstract
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) relies on gadolinium-based contrast agents (GBCAs) that have recently been found to accumulate in blood cells and various organs in patients with normal renal function. These concerns have motivated development of alternative manganese- and iron-based platforms. While macrophages are commonly evaluated when designing novel contrast agents, very few studies test contrast agent interactions with neutrophils. Here, we systematically evaluated how contrast agent design and metal content affect off-target innate immune responses in RAW 264.7 macrophages and primary murine neutrophils. Manganese oxide (MnO) and iron oxide (Fe3O4) nanoparticles were compared against metal-free blank nanoparticles and the clinical GBCA gadobutrol (Gadavist). Contrast agents were assessed for their ability to influence T1/T2 MRI signal, cell uptake, ROS generation, and innate immune activation. Gadavist had the highest MRI signal enhancement in macrophages (%ΔR1= 75%) and neutrophils (%ΔR1= 175%), confirming leukocyte uptake. Flow cytometry revealed low cell-associated nanoparticle fractions but higher activation marker expression in macrophages and higher ROS levels in neutrophils. However, metal content did not significantly elevate activation markers or ROS compared to blank nanoparticles. While metal oxide nanoparticles induced minimal changes in neutrophil and macrophage cytokine release, Gadavist significantly enhanced multiple inflammatory cytokines that drive immune cell recruitment. Herein, metal oxide nanoparticles had a more favorable acute immune compatibility than Gadavist. Reduced off-target immune cell interactions should be desirable to maximize target-to-background specificity as contrast agents move toward in vivo assessment. These results support evaluating MRI contrast performance alongside innate immune compatibility to enhance contrast efficacy and safety.

item.title: Remediation of Crude Oil-Contaminated Nigerian Soils by Microwave Heating
item.description:
Abstract
Oil spillage in Nigeria poses a significant threat to the environment, particularly in the Niger Delta region, which covers over 112,000 km2 and includes extensive areas that have become unsuitable for agriculture due to petroleum contamination. Microwave (MW) heating was investigated as a remediation technique for loamy, clay, and sand soils contaminated with 1.3–5.1% w/w crude oil by varying the treatment time and microwave power input. Using a microwave power of 0.8 kW and a treatment time of 420 s, more than 99% removal of solvent-extractable oil was achieved for the clay soil, while approximately 90% and less than 50% were obtained for the loamy and sand soils, respectively. The results demonstrate that remediation efficiency is strongly influenced by soil type, with clay soils exhibiting the highest oil removal under the investigated conditions. The findings suggest that soil water may play a critical role in microwave heating performance. Higher water content could increase the dielectric constant and dielectric loss factor of the soil, thereby promoting microwave energy absorption and potentially enhancing oil removal. In addition to water content, soil mineralogy and dielectric properties may significantly influence the oil removal process. Experimental results showed that increasing the water content of sand soil from 1.6% to 14% increased oil removal by 6%. Similarly, increasing the water content of loamy soil from 3.3% to 14% increased oil removal by 40%. These findings indicate that controlled water addition is an effective strategy for enhancing the microwave remediation of contaminated soils.

item.title: Characteristics and Physical–Environmental Coupling Evolution Model of Immediate On-Site Gas Desorption from Coal during Postmining Activities
item.description:
Abstract
Methane emissions from postmining activities originate from gas dissipation during transport and storage. This study investigates the immediate desorption characteristics and evolution laws of postmining coal through long-term tests on coarse particles and isothermal tests on fine particles under varying parameters. Results show a two-stage desorption process: a rapid linear growth stage posthoisting but before transport and processing, followed by a gradual decline and stabilization. The desorption volume exhibits a two-stage trend with coal rank, fluctuating from low- to high-metamorphic bituminous coal and increasing linearly from high-metamorphic bituminous coal to anthracite. Elevated ambient temperatures and smaller particle sizes significantly accelerate desorption rates. Integrating the Borges and exponential empirical models, a multiparameter coupled mathematical desorption model was constructed incorporating time, vitrinite reflectance, temperature, and particle size. The model shows excellent fitting performance for raw coal from typical mines (R2 > 0.98). This model effectively solves the challenge of accurately estimating initial gas loss during postmining activities. These findings provide a solid theoretical and experimental foundation for the measurement and accounting of postmining methane emissions.

item.title: Nutritional and Bioactive Valorization of Vegetables and Red Algae for Functional Food Innovation
item.description:
Abstract
In this study, a food-structured product resembling vegan seasoning cubes was developed utilizing vegetables, red algae (Gracilaria caudata and Hypnea pseudomusciformis) and their residues as bioactive, nutritional, and aromatic ingredients. The current demand for sustainable, healthy, plant-based diets highlights a market need for accessible and nutrient-rich culinary products that replace synthetic additives. The product was formulated by blending two solutions: an aqueous solution of Gracilaria (2%) and Hypnea (1%) extracts and a liquid concentrate of garlic, onion, chives, habanero pepper, parsley, and tomato (95%), obtained via 50% ethanolic extraction, combined with solid algal and vegetable residues (5%). The mixture was molded and cooled (4 °C/24 h). Fresh and freeze-dried samples were analyzed for color, antioxidant activity, rheology, chromatography, volatile compounds via GC-NOSE, and the bioaccessibility of Folin-Ciocalteu-reactive compounds and carbohydrates. The samples exhibited a neutral pH, greenish-yellow color, phenolic content ranging from 2.98 to 5.20 mg GAE/g, and an aroma profile characterized by acetaldehyde. Dissolution time in water was 0.97 min for the fresh product and 15.61 min for the freeze-dried version, due to molecular rearrangement. Bioaccessibility results demonstrated how the food matrix and processing affect nutrient release in the gastrointestinal tract. The highest Folin-Ciocalteu-reactive compound bioaccessibility for the fresh food-structured product occurred during the intestinal phase (79.5%), while the carbohydrates in the freeze-dried sample showed better bioaccessibility in the gastric phase (98.8%). This food-structured product serves a vegan ingredient with functional, practical, and sustainable characteristics, capable of enhancing the aroma, flavor, and bioactive compound content of foods.

item.title: Oleanolic Acid Liposomes Mitigate Knee Osteoarthritis by Remodeling Inflammatory Signaling and Cartilage Matrix Homeostasis
item.description:
Abstract
Knee osteoarthritis (KOA) is a chronic degenerative joint disease driven by persistent inflammation, synovial activation, and progressive cartilage matrix degradation, yet effective local therapeutic strategies remain limited. Oleanolic acid (OLA), a natural pentacyclic triterpenoid with anti-inflammatory and chondroprotective activities, is constrained by poor aqueous solubility and limited bioavailability. Here, we engineered OLA-loaded liposomes as a nanoscale delivery platform to improve the local applicability of OLA for KOA therapy. The liposomes were fabricated by thin-film hydration and systematically characterized by high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC), dynamic light scattering (DLS), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), and stability analysis. Their therapeutic performance was evaluated in a papain-induced rat KOA model and in lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-stimulated fibroblast-like synoviocytes (FLS) and RAW264.7 macrophages. Integrated network pharmacology and molecular docking identified the phosphoinositide 3-kinase/protein kinase B (PI3K/AKT) signaling axis as a potential regulatory pathway. In vivo and in vitro analyses demonstrated that OLA-loaded liposomes markedly reduced knee swelling, inhibited inflammatory cytokine production, attenuated synovial inflammation, and preserved cartilage integrity by restoring collagen II (COL II) expression and suppressing matrix metalloproteinase 13 (MMP13). These findings establish OLA-loaded liposomes as a promising nanoenabled therapeutic strategy for local KOA treatment and provide mechanistic insight into their anti-inflammatory and chondroprotective actions.

item.title: Using Convolutional Neural Networks to Detect Copper and Zinc Contamination through Cell Images of Egeria densa Leaf
item.description:
Abstract
Bioassays offer sensitive and cost-effective methods for detecting heavy metal contamination. In this study, we further integrate convolutional neural networks (CNNs) into bioassays, enabling high-throughput analysis. Specifically, we detect copper or zinc contamination through cell images of Egeria densa leaves. Four CNN models (InceptionV3, EfficientNetB1, ResNet152, and DenseNet121) achieved an accuracy of 99% in distinguishing among 0 ppm (control), 0.1 ppm copper, and 0.1 ppm zinc contamination. Other metrics, including precision, recall, and F1-score, all reached 0.99. Furthermore, when classifying three concentrations (0, 0.1, and 0.5 ppm) of copper or zinc contamination, ResNet152 achieved an accuracy of 98.4% for copper and 98.3% for zinc, and all models achieved an accuracy of over 93%, demonstrating their ability to distinguish between contamination severities. The results suggest that the combination of CNN with bioassays has the potential to monitor heavy metal contamination in the environment.

item.title: Transient Dynamics and Spatiotemporal Patterns of Gas Superposition in Multi-Shaft Asynchronous Reverse Ventilation
item.description:
Abstract
Reverse ventilation in multishaft mines is a complex transient process, referred to as asynchronous reverse ventilation. To clarify the transient dynamics and mechanisms of gas migration and superposition, we developed a 3D high-fidelity dynamic simulation model of the ventilation network. Taking Shaqu No. 2 Mine’s two-wing ventilation system as a case study and using the TF1M3D platform, we simulated dynamic parameter variations and gas migration superposition during asynchronous reversal between the return-air inclined shaft and the Baijiapo return-air vertical shaft. The results show that two-wing asynchronous reversal adjustments induced air-volume variations of less than 9.2% in the return airways and less than 17.6% at the working face. Analysis of the impact of reverse ventilation on gas superposition and exceedance revealed distinct spatiotemporal patterns. At the 4903 working face, the gas concentration fluctuated, peaking at 1.69% at 510 s due to reversal superposition, and at 1.70% at 1550 s after ventilation restoration, exceeding the limit. At the 5303 working face, it peaked at 0.81% at 780 s and 0.95% at 1500 s postrestoration, approaching the thresholds. Fan adjustments during two-wing asynchronous reversals caused gas-concentration fluctuations at each working face, and mining haulage roadways also exhibited fluctuations and exceedance events.

item.title: Synthesis of a High-Performance VPEG-Based Polycarboxylate Superplasticizer via Copolymerization and Its Effects on Cement Performance
item.description:
Abstract
A high-performance polycarboxylate superplasticizer (VAP-MHC) was developed via free-radical copolymerization of 4-hydroxybutyl vinyl polyoxyethylene ether (VPEG) and acrylic acid (AA), a process critically mediated by a redox initiation system (H2O2/ascorbic acid) and 3-mercaptopropionic acid as a chain transfer agent, with polyethylene glycol-600 incorporated as a nonreactive polymeric additive. This copolymerization strategy, distinct from conventional homopolymerization or simple blending approaches, enables precise architectural control over the polymer backbone, affording the VAP-MHC superplasticizer with exceptional dispersibility and robust slump retention. Under optimized conditions, the synthesized VAP-MHC achieved a cement paste flow of 273 mm and a 28-day compressive strength of 59.7 MPa, significantly outperforming commercial counterparts in both initial fluidity and mechanical development. The enhanced performance is attributed to the synergistic interplay between the VPEG-AA copolymer architecture and the multifunctional additive system, which effectively addresses the persistent trade-off between water reduction and workability loss─a challenge that continues to limit conventional superplasticizers in practical applications.

item.title: Extraction, Stability, and Statistical Optimization of Pigments from Mango ( Mangifera indica L.) Peel as Sustainable Colorants for Cellulosic Fibers
item.description:
Abstract
Replacing synthetic dyes with natural alternatives derived from agro-industrial waste is crucial for the circular economy and the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals. This study investigates the potential of mango peel (Mangifera indica L.) as a source of natural dye for cotton, focusing on pigment stability and the optimization of processing conditions. The alcoholic extract was physically and chemically characterized, confirming the presence of polyphenols and flavonoids responsible for the yellowish color and antioxidant activity. Stability studies revealed that the pigments are sensitive to alkaline conditions, high temperatures, and prolonged UV irradiation, indicating specific storage guidelines. The dyeing process was optimized using a 2k factorial design, evaluating color variation (CIELAB system) and dye bath exhaustion efficiency. The results demonstrated that bath temperature, extract concentration, and contact time are statistically significant factors for dyeing efficacy. The optimized conditions yielded consistent and reproducible coloration, positioning mango peel extract as a viable, sustainable alternative for the textile industry with the potential to reduce the environmental impact associated with conventional dyes.

item.title: Disc-Shaped Particles with Cellulose Nanocrystals and Poly(ethylene glycol)-Based Polymers as Phase-Change Materials
item.description:
Abstract
We have previously reported that disc-shaped particles are fabricated from cellulose nanocrystals (CNCs) and polyethylene glycol diacrylate (PEGDA) through reorganization in a solvent. The disc-shaped particles, which encapsulate PEGDA with outer-segregated CNCs, can be a promising heat storage material through the phase transition of PEGDA around 50 °C, based on the general view that they have a larger specific surface area than spherical ones, with the assistance of outer-segregated CNCs. In this study, we have clarified the thermal properties of the disc-shaped particles and proved that these discs are promising phase-change materials (PCM): First, the PEGDA crystals in the discs are easier to crystallize during the cooling process than in the bulk state, leading to suppressed supercooling, reasonably due to the larger specific surface area, and the other is that the powder of the disc particles does not melt in appearance above the melting temperature, which leads to a stand-alone leakage-free PCM.

item.title: Data-Driven Discovery of High-Performance EOR Surfactants: Coupling Molecular Dynamics with Active Learning
item.description:
Abstract
Chemical Enhanced Oil Recovery (EOR) is a central route to maximizing hydrocarbon recovery from mature reservoirs. Although its field-scale success depends on several factors─including surfactant cost, adsorption and retention on the reservoir rock, solubility, and phase behavior─achieving a low oil–water interfacial tension (IFT) is a key enabling requirement. However, the design of surfactants meeting this requirement is impeded by the vast combinatorics of the chemical space and the prohibitive cost of traditional trial-and-error screening. In this study, we present a synergistic materials informatics framework that integrates Machine Learning (ML) and Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations within an Active Learning (AL) workflow to accelerate surfactant discovery. Unlike static screening approaches, our methodology utilizes MD simulations as a high-fidelity oracle, iteratively labeling a subset of candidates to update a regressor, enabling the identification of high-performance surfactants from the PubChem database. Through this workflow, we identified Dodecylammonium Chloride (DDACl) as a top candidate; subsequent high-fidelity MD simulations confirmed a very low IFT at maximum surface coverage, outperforming widely used analogs such as Cetyltrimethylammonium Bromide (CTAB). We validated these computational findings through experimental tensiometry, confirming the efficacy of DDACl in reducing IFT in several oils with varying API gravities. The convergence of theoretical predictions with experimental results underscores the power of this data-driven framework to overcome the “small data” bottleneck in materials science, offering a scalable pathway for the data-driven discovery of surfactants with low oil–water IFT as candidates for EOR formulation development.

item.title: Salicylamide Derivatives Inhibit Multiple Picornavirus Infections through Early Endosome Neutralization
item.description:
Abstract
The global resurgence of picornaviruses highlights an urgent need for broad-spectrum antivirals. Here, we screened 102 salicylamide derivatives, identifying HJW1107 and CZY1111 as inhibitors with submicromolar IC50 values. Time-of-addition and RNA transfection assays confirmed that these derivatives target early infection stages rather than virus replication or assembly. Mechanistically, HJW1107 and CZY1111 exhibit protonophore-like activity that neutralizes endosomal acidification, trapping internalized virions within EEA1-positive early endosomal compartments. This arrest prevents pH-dependent viruses from undergoing uncoating after endocytosis required for virus replication. These results demonstrate that optimizing the salicylamide scaffold to disrupt endosomal maturation offers a therapeutic strategy against acidification-dependent picornaviruses, potentially imposing a higher barrier to resistance than direct targeting of highly variable viral proteins.

item.title: Comparative Antifungal Activity of Metal–Organic Frameworks (MOFs) with Different Metal Centers and Structural Dimensionalities against Candida albicans
item.description:
Abstract
Fungal infections, such as those caused byCandida albicans (C. albicans), represent a growing global health threat due to rising antifungal resistance and limited antifungal therapy options. Porous materials, including metal–organic frameworks (MOFs), have shown promise as antifungal agents, but the reported studies are difficult to compare due to the different metrics used to evaluate antifungal activity. Herein, we present a comparative study of a series of 1,3,5-triformylphloroglucinol (Tp)-based MOFs containing Cu, Mn, Fe, and Ni nodes, aiming to elucidate how metal-dependent characteristics, together with inherent framework features, influence their physicochemical properties and antifungal activity. While all four materials show better antifungal activity than the corresponding metal salts, MnTp and FeTp were the most effective at inhibiting planktonicC. albicanscells with >50% decrease in viability over 24 h, likely due to their rich intracellular redox activity.C. albicans biofilm formation was most effectively inhibited by NiTp with >60% biofilm inhibition over the same time period, an observation that we attribute to the highest ζ-potential of NiTp in the MOF series, to the nonendogenous nature of Ni2+ linked to the extracellular matrix trapping of Ni2+ ions, and to a small proportion of Ni2+ release. Ultimately, this study calls for further systematic investigation of MOFs as potential materials for the treatment of fungal infections and for more consistent reporting of antifungal activity in the literature.

item.title: Soil-Plant Nutrient Dynamics and Edaphic Constraints of Cashew Genotypes in the Amazon Savanna
item.description:
Abstract
To guide sustainable cashew cultivation, this study evaluated the nutritional dynamics and environmental interactions of five cashew clones across two contrasting pedological environments (clay-rich vs highly sandy) acting as extreme case studies within the Amazon Savanna (Roraima). By analyzing soil profiles (0–40 cm) and foliar nutrient concentrations, we identified extreme spatial heterogeneity. In the clay-rich soils of Normandia, severe acidity and high exchangeable aluminum were observed, alongside higher soil organic matter (SOM) and significantly greater foliar K accumulation across all clones, while N and P increases were genotype-specific. Conversely, the highly sandy soils (>80% sand) of Bonfim exhibited characteristics associated with nutrient leaching risks. Principal Component Analysis explained 81.6% of the data set’s total variance (PC1:69.3%; PC2:12.3%), revealing an absolute clustering of samples by cultivation environment rather than by genotype. This suggests that local edaphic conditions strongly shape the crop’s nutritional signature. We hypothesize that SOM acts as a key buffer in these environments, potentially mitigating Al stress and reducing nutrient loss. Clone BRS 274 demonstrated stable nutritional performance in Normandia, while clone CCP 09 exhibited physiological responses adapted to the sandy soils of Bonfim.

item.title: Wasp Nest as a Natural Cellulose–Protein Biocomposite Material: Integrated Investigation of Structural Properties, Microbiota and Uranium Adsorption Performance
item.description:
Abstract
This research explores the structural attributes, microbial composition, and potential application of wasp nest material (WN) as a natural biocomposite for uranium adsorption from aqueous solutions. The physicochemical properties of WN were characterized using FTIR, SEM, EDX, BET, and XPS methodologies. The study systematically assessed the impact of variables such as initial uranium concentration, pH, contact time, temperature, and adsorbent dosage on the adsorption efficiency. The adsorption isotherm adhered to the Langmuir model, demonstrating a maximum adsorption capacity of 1.169 mol kg–1. The Freundlich heterogeneity factor was calculated to be 0.43, while the D–R model indicated an adsorption energy of 10.4 kJ mol–1, pointing to chemisorption. Kinetic analysis revealed that the Elovich model best described the data, with an initial adsorption rate of 114.4 mol kg–1 min–1. The positive enthalpy values confirmed the endothermic nature of the adsorption, and the negative Gibbs free energy values suggested spontaneity. XPS analysis confirmed the adsorption of U(VI) on WN, with U 4f 7/2 and U 4f 5/2 peaks at 381.8 and 392.6 eV, respectively, indicative of uranyl species and their chemical interaction with oxygen-containing functional groups on the biocomposite surface. The microbial community within WN may influence the adsorbent’s performance by secreting extracellular polymeric substances (EPS), potentially enhancing uranium binding through enrichment of functional groups. These findings underscore the potential of wasp nest material, a natural and environmentally friendly cellulose-based protein-containing biocomposite, as a viable option for uranium removal from aqueous solutions.

item.title: Detection of Antipoly(ethylene glycol) IgM in Immune Serum by Oligo(ethylene glycol)-Conjugated Cello-oligosaccharide Assemblies
item.description:
Abstract
Adsorbing antibodies of interest onto solid supports displaying corresponding antigens is an efficient strategy for their subsequent purification and detection. We have previously demonstrated the potential of water-dispersible, antibiofouling, and designable cello-oligosaccharide assemblies for antibody detection via enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). However, whether antigen-conjugated cello-oligosaccharide assemblies can detect specific antibodies contained in immune serum remains unexplored. In this study, we demonstrate the utility of oligo(ethylene glycol) (OEG)-conjugated cello-oligosaccharide assemblies for detecting antipoly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) immunoglobulin M (IgM) in serum from immunized animals. Mouse sera containing anti-PEG IgMs, induced by immunogenic polymers, were utilized for evaluation. ELISA results revealed that anti-PEG IgMs in the serum with no heat-inactivation or depletion were successfully detected by cello-oligosaccharide assemblies displaying OEG chains with at least three repeating ethylene glycol units. ELISAs using a series of cello-oligosaccharide assemblies displaying OEG chains indicated that the conjugation rate of OEG chains influences anti-PEG IgM binding. Furthermore, increasing the serum concentration led to enhanced detection efficacy for anti-PEG IgM, likely due to the superior antibiofouling properties of the cello-oligosaccharide assemblies, which minimize nonspecific adsorption of serum proteins. The concentration of the assemblies also significantly influenced the detection efficacy. Additionally, 7 days after a single intravenous injection of OEG-conjugated cello-oligosaccharide assemblies without micrometer-scale aggregates, ELISA signals for IgMs against PEG chains, OEG chains, and cello-oligosaccharide moieties were comparable to those of saline-treated controls. These findings demonstrated that OEG-conjugated cello-oligosaccharide assemblies hold considerable potential for the detection of anti-PEG IgMs in immune serum with no heat-inactivation or depletion.

item.title: Cationic Phenylpyridine Labeling for Improved Oligosaccharide and Glycan Analysis by Capillary Electrophoresis with LED-Induced Fluorescence Detection
item.description:
Abstract
Capillary electrophoresis with laser-induced fluorescence detection (CE/LIF) is a powerful technique for analyzing glycans. However, it requires derivatization with a fluorescent compound to enhance both electrophoretic mobility and detection sensitivity simultaneously. The widely used labeling reagent 8-aminopyrene-1,3,6-trisulfonic acid (APTS) suffers from several limitations, including relatively low labeling efficiency and poor compatibility with mass spectrometry (MS), highlighting the need for improved alternatives. In this work, we designed and synthesized a novel cationic fluorescent label based on a phenylpyridine scaffold incorporating hydrazide functionality for efficient oligosaccharide and glycan derivatization via hydrazone formation. To fully exploit its fluorescence characteristics, we also optimized the capillary electrophoresis system by modifying the LED-induced fluorescence (LED-IF) detector through systematic evaluation of excitation LEDs and emission filters, resulting in substantially improved detection sensitivity. The optimized labeling, separation, and detection conditions enabled sensitive analysis of released glycans from various glycoproteins with detection limits in the nanomolar concentration range. The combination of this new phenylpyridine-based fluorescent label with the enhanced CE/LED-IF detection platform significantly improves the analytical performance of CE for glycan analysis and provides a more sensitive, robust, and versatile approach for comprehensive oligosaccharide and glycan characterization.

item.title: Ultrasound-Assisted Extraction of Bioactive Compounds from Acmella oleracea L. Leaves: Optimization by Response Surface Methodology and Comparison with Percolation
item.description:
Abstract
The extract of Acmella oleracea L. (jambu) contains significant amounts of spilanthol and phenolic compounds, which have wide-ranging applications in the cosmetic and pharmaceutical industries. The objective of this study was to optimize ultrasound-assisted extraction (UAE) of hydroethanolic extracts from A. oleracea L. using a Box–Behnken factorial design combined with response surface methodology and to directly compare the results with those of the conventional percolation method. The effects of the ethanol-to-water ratio, extraction time, and solid-to-solvent ratio were evaluated on yield, total phenolic content, total flavonoid content, and antioxidant activity. In addition, Fourier-transform infrared (FT-IR) spectroscopy was used for chemical characterization and extraction monitoring. For UAE, the optimal conditions established were an ethanol/water ratio of 47:53 (v/v), an extraction time of 13.2 min, and a solid-to-solvent ratio of 1:10 (m/v). In contrast, optimal percolation yielded an 11.03% recovery using a 70:30 (v/v) ethanol/water ratio. UAE provided a significantly higher yield (17.61%) and better recovery of bioactive compounds, as well as superior antioxidant activity in all assays. FT-IR analysis confirmed the preservation of functional groups, demonstrating that UAE optimizes the recovery of oxygen-containing compounds. It is concluded that UAE is a green, rapid, and sustainable alternative that maximizes the potential of A. oleracea L. for future cosmetic and nutritional formulations.

item.title: Development and In Vitro Evaluation of Kaempferol-Loaded Liposomes in LN-229 Glioblastoma Cells: Potency, Selectivity, and Modulation of ROS-Dependent Cytotoxicity
item.description:
Abstract
Glioblastoma multiforme has a median survival of 12–15 months despite multimodal treatment, due to blood-brain barrier impermeability limiting CNS drug bioavailability. Liposomal nanoformulations circumvent this barrier while offering tunable surface chemistry and amphiphilic drug-loading capacity. Here, we report encapsulation of kaempferol, a dietary flavonoid, within phosphatidylcholine-cholesterol liposomes (Lip-KPF) and evaluate cytotoxic activity against LN-229 glioblastoma cells relative to free kaempferol (KPF) and puromycin aminonucleoside (Puro-A). LCMS confirmed 56% encapsulation efficiency; dynamic light scattering yielded a zeta potential of −15.32 ± 0.83 mV, mean particle size of 200.44 ± 12.22 nm, and PDI of 0.29 ± 0.06, with 31P NMR confirming a multilamellar structure. Lip-KPF potency against LN-229 cells increased progressively across 24–72 h, peaking at 72 h (19.880 μM) with significantly lower IC50 values than free KPF (p < 0.001), while maintaining lower astrocyte toxicity. Selectivity indices for Lip-KPF exceeded 1 at every time point, widening over time. Cell death was confirmed by TUNEL assay and phase-contrast microscopy. RT-qPCR revealed concurrent BAX and TP53 upregulation alongside CASP3/CASP7 suppression in both groups, with no significant difference between KPF and Lip-KPF; ELISA corroborated CASP3 suppression, consistent with a possible caspase-independent death mechanism. In a preliminary antioxidant rescue assay, pretreatment did not significantly alter KPF-induced cytotoxicity but significantly increased it in Lip-KPF-treated cells, indicating a cytotoxic mechanism independent of the ROS pathway contributing to free KPF’s activity. These findings support Lip-KPF as a candidate for continued preclinical investigation in LN-229 glioblastoma cells.

item.title: Enhanced Shale-Swelling Inhibition and Plugging Efficiency in Water-Based Drilling Muds by Graphene Oxide Nanocomposites
item.description:
Abstract
Shale formations pose significant challenges to conventional water-based muds (WBMs) due to fluid invasion, cuttings dispersion, shale hydration and swelling, leading to wellbore instability. To address these challenges, a novel dodecylamine graphene oxide nanocomposite (DAGONC) was synthesized as a shale inhibitor. Its performance in mitigating shale hydration and enhancing the plugging efficiency of WBMs was systematically evaluated through linear swelling, API filtration, uniaxial compressive strength, contact angle, atomic force microscopy (AFM), and BET analyses. The performance of DAGONC was compared with KCl and partially hydrolyzed polyacrylamide (PHPA) inhibitors. FTIR, XRD, and FESEM confirmed successful synthesis and characterization of DAGONC. The linear swelling test showed that 0.5 wt % DAGONC reduced shale swelling to 3.6%, compared to 9.8% and 6.0% for 5 wt % KCl and 5 wt % PHPA, respectively. In addition, shale cuttings recovery at 250 °F reached to 96% with DAGONC, outperforming KCl (84%) and PHPA (90.7%). The findings showed that incorporating DAGONC into WBMs reduced fluid loss by 55% under LPLT conditions and by 38% at HPHT conditions, showing a significant enhancement in filtration control. DAGONCS increased shale surface hydrophobicity, with a contact angle of 85.6°, versus 54.6° and 63.1° for KCl and PHPA, respectively. AFM revealed a thin and homogeneous DAGONC layer bridging pores and cracks, while BET analysis indicated a reduced surface area to 6.63 m2, confirming strong interaction between DAGONC and the shale matrix. The flexible sheet-like structure forms a continuous protective film, effectively sealing pores, inhibiting water invasion, and maintaining shale integrity. These findings suggest that DAGONC can improve WBM performance and contribute to enhanced wellbore stability in shale formations.

item.title: UV-Electrochemical Catalytic Oxidation of Quinoline-Containing Wastewater Using an IrO 2 -Based Anode: COD Reduction, Degradation Kinetics, and Transformation Pathway
item.description:
Abstract
Quinoline is a refractory nitrogen-containing pollutant commonly found in coal chemical, coking, pharmaceutical, and dye wastewater. Although advanced oxidation processes have shown potential for quinoline removal, an integrated understanding of pollutant removal, COD reduction, degradation kinetics, and intermediate transformation in UV-electrochemical systems remains limited. In this study, simulated quinoline-containing wastewater was treated using a dual-wavelength UV-electrochemical catalytic oxidation system equipped with a commercial Ti/IrO2 anode and a stainless-steel cathode. The effects of current density, electrolysis time, NaCl concentration, and initial pH on quinoline degradation were systematically investigated, while COD reduction, degradation kinetics, and intermediate transformation were further evaluated by HPLC and GC-MS. Under a current density of 30 mA/cm2, NaCl concentration of 0.5 mol/L, near-neutral initial pH, and reaction time of 90 min, quinoline and COD removal efficiencies reached 87.2% and 84.7%, respectively. Further increases in current density or reaction time produced only limited additional improvement under the investigated conditions. Control experiments showed higher quinoline removal in the combined process than in either individual process. Kinetic analysis showed that quinoline degradation could be adequately described by an apparent pseudo-first-order model. HPLC and GC-MS analyses indicated a proposed transformation pathway involving hydroxylation and quinolinone formation, followed by cleavage of the aromatic and heterocyclic structures and subsequent oxidation to small-molecule organic acids. These results provide an integrated evaluation of quinoline removal, COD reduction, kinetic behavior, and intermediate transformation, thereby providing a basis for further optimization of UV-electrochemical treatment of quinoline-containing wastewater.

item.title: Docking Simulation and Artificial-Intelligence-Assisted Molecularly Imprinted Polymer Electrochemical Sensor for the Detection of Cancer Biomarkers
item.description:
Abstract
Cancer remains one of the leading life-threatening diseases worldwide, and therefore, early stage detection of cancer biomarkers is vital for effective diagnosis and treatment planning.
